articles.summary: Amazon will own just under 15% of Anthropic after the IPO, with the option to go much higher. Google is a close second with holdings of nearly 14%.
articles.excerpt: Anthropic on Tuesday disclosed more details about the biggest investment agreements with major cloud providers Amazon and Google. While we already knew that Amazon stood to make a killing on its Anthropic investments from the IPO, Anthropic revealed that Amazon’s total stake will come in at just shy of 15% (14.7% to be exact). Even more interesting is that Amazon could have, if it wished, owned an even bigger share of the company. When Amazon invested billions in Anthropic in 2023 and 2024 (long before Claude Code took the enterprise world by storm, back in the days when Anthropic looked like it would forever be a speck in OpenAI’s shadow), the cloud giant obtained promissory notes that could convert into equity. These notes carry conversion prices of about $2.09 or $5.05 per share, depending on the year of investment. Amazon has opted to convert a chunk of them as part of the IPO into a special class of non-voting shares that will give it about 15% ownership. (The shares can receive dividends and convert to standard voting Class A shares when sold, the filing says.) But it has also opted to hold on to billions of dollars’ worth of the notes for now. If it converted them all right now, it would own just under 24% of Anthropic (23.8% to be precise). articles.summary: The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis.
articles.excerpt: Model ML, a London-based startup that uses AI to automate work traditionally performed by junior bankers and consultants, including building financial models, preparing pitch decks, and writing due diligence reports, has raised $250 million in Series B funding at a $1.5 billion valuation. The new round, which comes a year after its $75 million Series A round was announced, was co-led by General Atlantic and earlier backer QED Investors. Brothers Chaz and Arnie Englander co-founded the three-year-old startup after previously co-founding two other companies, including Fat Llama, a peer-to-peer rental marketplace acquired by Swedish rival Hygglo for $41.5 million in 2022. Model ML develops AI agents that integrate with clients’ systems, data, and tools, including Excel and PowerPoint. The startup says its agents understand the full context of deals that bankers and consultants are working on and can automatically update financial models and presentations when new developments affect their analysis. Other startups automating the routine, repetitive tasks for investment bankers and management consultants include Hebbia and Rogo, which raised $160 million at a $2 billion valuation in April. Anthropic and OpenAI have also built tools for financial professionals, but Model ML says it runs on open source models and that doing so allows it to operate at about 2% of the cost of frontier models while delivering faster results. articles.excerpt: Retailers and brands rushing to deploy AI agents risk creating a new generation of disconnected technology, unless they address the product data, governance, and operating models required to make multiple agents work together, according to a new whitepaper from Akeneo . The Agentic PIM Playbook examines the transitional phase as organisations move beyond individual AI experiments and begin deploying multiple specialised agents across the product lifecycle. Akeneo argues that while the first AI agent may solve a relatively straightforward use case, the challenge changes fundamentally as organisations deploy more of them. As the whitepaper states, “Your first agent is a use case. Your tenth is an operating model.” The paper identifies ten potential agents spanning the product lifecycle, including product modelling, supplier data, enrichment, content creation, localisation, asset intelligence, quality and compliance, activation, market intelligence, and insights. While individual AI agents are likely to become widely available, Akeneo argues this accessibility to the technology itself will therefore provide relatively little competitive differentiation. What will matter is whether agents can share trusted data, business rules, workflows, and governance. The warning comes as retailers and brands increasingly explore agentic AI to automate activities that have traditionally required significant manual intervention. Rather than relying on a single general-purpose AI assistant, Akeneo expects product teams will increasingly work alongside fleets of specialised agents, each responsible for different elements of managing, enriching and distributing product information. articles.title: Inside L’Oréal-owned La Roche-Posay’s BEMT launch: ‘It’s enabling us to have a new conversation with new consumers’
articles.summary: U.S. sunscreen manufacturers are currently navigating the biggest change in the market in nearly 25 years. In June, the FDA approved its first new sunscreen filter in 25 years with the addition of BEMT, an ingredient that’s been widely available in Europe since 2000. Glossy sat down with the gm and formulator behind La Roche-Posay, L’Oréal Group’s sunscreen leader, to learn how the brand is leveraging the new filter to grow awareness and sales.
articles.excerpt: U.S. sunscreen manufacturers are navigating the biggest market change in nearly 25 years. In June, the U.S. Food & Drug Administration approved its first new sunscreen filter in 25 years: bemotrizinol, or BEMT, an ingredient that’s been widely available in Europe and Asia since 2000 and 2002, respectively. The filter has been heralded online for its remarkably lightweight, smooth feel; larger molecule size; and ability to protect against both UVA, the rays that age skin, and UVB, the rays that burn skin. “We love that we now get a new tool, and it’s not just a flash in the pan because it’s the new thing on the block,” Brian Bodnar, L’Oréal Group principal scientist of photoprotection, North America, told Glossy. “It’s important that we protect against both UVA and UVB, which is a little bit more difficult when you don’t have a large UV filter toolset to use as we might have in other countries.” BEMT offers wider photo protection than U.S. filters like avobenzone or homosalate. “We [have] really lacked this middle ground [in the U.S.], right in between UVA and UVB,” he said. “It’s a wavelength area known as UVA 2, a short wavelength right in between, and BEMT helps us fill in the gap.” What’s more, BEMT is made from a larger molecule than other chemical filters available in the U.S., which means less of the formula soaks into the bloodstream, a mounting concern among some consumers who avoid endocrine disruptors or are prone to irritation from sunscreen. “It really doesn’t go into the skin almost at all in most formulations, so you don’t have to worry about that too much,” Bodnar said. Grace Riggenbach, gm of La Roche-Posay, told Glossy that BEMT allows for better hydration and a more lightweight, elegant formula, all of which the company will lean into across marketing.

articles.summary: Nearly one in three fraud prevention pros say minimizing costs outweighs the risk of loss. The post Is Fraud Prevention Worth the Cost? appeared first on Practical Ecommerce .
articles.excerpt: Few things frustrate ecommerce businesses more than fraud, especially when ignoring it can seem like the better option. Yes, sometimes preventing fraud — software, staff time — can cost more than the crime itself, forcing merchants to balance security with expenses and customer experience. The Merchant Risk Council is a global non-profit organization for payments and fraud prevention professionals, founded in 2000. In December 2025, MRC surveyed members across 37 countries, categories, and company sizes, and received 1,278 responses. The results, published in MRC’s “ 2026 Global Ecommerce Payments & Fraud Report,” found that 29% of respondents identified minimizing operational costs as their top fraud-management priority, up from 10% two years ago. The finding suggests that stopping fraud is no longer the only objective for nearly one in three members who evidently assess whether prevention produces a financial return. Ecommerce businesses pay to prevent fraud in several ways, not all of them obvious. Some attacks create costs without attempting a purchase. Card testing, for example, involves criminals submitting stolen payment credentials to determine which ones work. Thousands of attempts can burden checkout systems and attract scrutiny from payment providers. Refund abuse creates another expense. To evaluate a claim, a merchant might spend time examining photographs, reviewing delivery records, and contacting the customer. The MRC estimated that resolving a first-party dispute, which can involve a legitimate cardholder disputing an authorized transaction, costs merchants more than $80 on average. The changes came with United’s announcement that it is restricting unauthorized third-party AI agents on its own platforms and through travel agencies and booking sites. The airline updated its contract of carriage (the passenger agreement that comes with buying a ticket) on the same day. For those on SEO and ecommerce teams who have created their own rules for AI agents, the airline’s rules are an example of what a big company has done. The rules for the AI agents can be found in both the terms and conditions and the contract. As of Nov. 14, United’s robots.txt file named no crawlers or agents for any AI. The announcement from United says that sharing account login credentials with an outside third-party AI assistant can expose customers’ sensitive information. articles.title: ‘We’re not trying to be TwitchTok’: Twitch adds new short-form video feature
articles.summary: Twitch is swinging big with a new short-form content push that should help more creators get discovered on-platform.
articles.excerpt: Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit For Twitch streamers, on-platform discoverability has always been a major issue. Twitch has tried to address this, with mixed success. Now, the platform is making its biggest swing yet. Starting early next year, Twitch will let creators upload short-form videos made outside the platform. Announced during the keynote at TwitchCon 2026 in San Diego, the move is aimed at improving on-platform discovery and creating more ad inventory. Twitch’s goal isn’t to make clips into a TikTok-like destination, execs say, but to help viewers discover creators and tune into their livestreams, where creators make most of their money. The new uploads build on Twitch’s existing Clips tools, which have let creators and viewers clip livestreams and share them on-platform for more than a decade. But clips made or shared outside the platform are now a central part of creator culture . “It’s a smart thing for them to do. You want to follow your favorite Twitch creators but you aren’t able to catch them live at that moment, so you’re going to TikTok or you’re watching old uploads on YouTube,” said Eric Bogard, CEO of UnderCurrent Talent.
